question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+2x+3 & =-({x}^{2}-2x)+3 \\  & =-(({x}^{2}-2x+1)-1)+3 \\  & =-((x-1)^{2}-1)+3 \\  & =-(x-1)^{2}+1+3 \\  & =4-(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x+3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{4-(x-1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{4(1-(x-1)^{2}/4)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{4}\cdot \sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}/{2}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x-1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(\frac{x-1}{2}).$

So, let's perform the substitution

$$
u=\frac{x-1}{2}.
$$

Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\text{d}u.
$$

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $1-\sqrt{3}$ | $1+\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{3}{\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+2x+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-((x-1)/2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\text{d}u \\  & =3{\int }_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2} \\  & =3(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})) \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{3}-(-\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
